newsitem.title: USA: Clinton sees continuity in U.S.-China relations.
newsitem.headline: Clinton sees continuity in U.S.-China relations.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said Thursday he expected continuity in U.S. relations with China following the death of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping.
"We expect basic continuity here," Clinton told reporters at the White House.
"Perhaps mindful of some of the problems they've had in their long history in transitions, Deng Ziaoping set in motion a process that has been well under way for more than two years now," he said.

Noting that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was due to visit China later this week and Vice President Al Gore is scheduled to go to Beijing next month to prepare a presidential summit later this year, Clinton said the United States would continue to engage China while honestly airing differences.
"I you imagine what the world will look like 30 years from now, 40 years from now, we can do nothing other than what we are doing. It is the right thing to do," he said.

Winston Lord, former ambassador to Beijing and former assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs, said in a CNN interview that the United States should engage China "without illusion, without naivety but with a real sense that we've got to engage this emerging power."

He also expected continuity in the short term, noting that Jiang Zemin was expected to be ratified as China's president by the Communist Party Congress next October. This would confirm him as "first among equals".

"Jiang has consolidated his position and I've noticed over the last three or four years a growing self confidence. I've been in all the meetings between him and President Clinton...and he has grown in self confidence and assertiveness which I think reflects a consolidation of power," he said.

But Jiang would be operating in a collective leadership. "He can't make decisions on his own like Deng Xiaoping could or Mao Zedong before him. He's got to form consensus so he has a little bit less latitude. We don't have a strong emperor now. We have a more traditional technocratic leader," Lord said.

In the longer term, Lord said, China needed to resolve the key questions of how much political openness should go along with economic reform and how it should handle growing disparities between rich and poor.
